title: Class 11 Chemistry — Organic Chemistry Foundations Study Guide
notes: Organic chemistry primarily studies carbon compounds, especially those with C–C or C–H frameworks. Some simple carbon compounds such as carbon oxides, carbonates and carbides are conventionally treated as inorganic. The separate study reflects the diversity of carbon compounds, catenation and tetravalency—not a claim that all organic substances come from living organisms.

Neutral carbon commonly forms four covalent bonds. Strong C–C bonding permits chains, branches and rings (catenation). Classify skeletons as open-chain or cyclic, saturated or unsaturated, and aliphatic or aromatic. A homologous series has a common functional group and general formula; successive members differ by –CH₂– and show related chemistry with gradual physical-property changes.

Functional groups give families characteristic chemistry: –OH alcohol, –CHO aldehyde, >C=O ketone, –COOH carboxylic acid, –NH₂ amine and –X halo. Molecular formula counts atoms; expanded structural formula shows bonds; condensed formula compresses groups (CH₃CH₂OH); bond-line formula uses vertices/endpoints for carbon and usually omits carbon-bound hydrogens. Verify each carbon has valence four and heteroatoms have plausible valence.

Cracking breaks larger hydrocarbons into smaller molecules, often producing useful alkanes and alkenes. Reforming rearranges or cyclizes hydrocarbons to improve gasoline quality. Octane number measures resistance to knocking in spark-ignition engines relative to reference fuels; it is not energy content. Cetane number indicates ignition quality/delay in compression-ignition engines; higher cetane generally means shorter ignition delay. Additives must meet safety and environmental requirements.
keyPoints: Organic chemistry is not simply chemistry of substances made by organisms.
Carbon tetravalency and catenation explain extensive structural diversity.
Successive homologous-series members differ by CH₂ and share a functional group.
Bond-line notation omits carbon labels and most attached hydrogens; valence still must balance.
Octane describes knock resistance in spark engines; cetane describes ignition delay in diesel engines.
practiceQuestions: Explain carbon's structural diversity using tetravalency and catenation.
Identify functional groups in CH₃CH₂OH, CH₃CHO, CH₃COCH₃ and CH₃COOH.
Draw expanded, condensed and bond-line representations of butane and propan-2-ol.
Distinguish cracking from reforming and octane number from cetane number.
summary: Read organic structures by identifying the carbon skeleton and functional group, then translate between formula styles. Industrial fuel processes and ratings describe distinct aspects of hydrocarbon performance.
